title: Kyiv's baptism (988)
hook: Prince Vladimir's people are baptized in the Dnieper, a shared root of Orthodox and Eastern Catholics

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charlemagne, a crown in Rome and schools beside it. Your line was crowns and cathedrals. Where did you invite instead of insist? Day seven hundred sixty-four.

A wide river runs past a city on high bluffs. On the bank stand priests in vestments, come from the Greek lands to the south. Into the water walk the people of Kyiv, the old chronicle says, some up to their necks, some to their chests, the young ones near the shore, parents holding their babies. The priests stand and say the prayers over them. A whole city, baptized together in the Dnieper. Today, Kyiv's baptism.
screen: `A RIVER BELOW THE BLUFFS.` → `PRIESTS ON THE BANK.` → `A CITY IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Our main source is the old chronicle of Kyiv, written by monks, sometimes called the Tale of Bygone Years. It tells the story of Vladimir, grand prince of Kyiv. It says his envoys came back from a liturgy in the great church of Constantinople and said they hadn't known whether they were in heaven or on earth, only that God dwells there among people. The beauty of the worship moved them. Next, the prince. The chronicle says Vladimir himself was baptized, married a sister of the emperors in Constantinople, and came home with priests. Then he sent word through the city: anyone, rich or poor, who did not come to the river would be counted the prince's enemy. That was a command, not an invitation, and it's worth hearing honestly, the day after Charlemagne. The chronicle says the people came gladly. Whatever was in each heart, they came. The chronicle tells the scene with real tenderness: people standing in the water, the priests praying, and Vladimir, it says, glad that he and his people knew God. Now, why it matters on this path. This baptism is a shared root. Orthodox churches of Ukraine, Russia and Belarus trace their faith to that river, and so does the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, which prays in the Eastern way and is in communion with Rome. Both remember Vladimir as a saint. One river, two families who each call it the beginning. The Gospels use the same Greek word, baptizo, when Jesus sends the apostles out to baptize all nations. The carry is the plain picture: baptized in the river. A people's faith beginning not in a building, but in water, out under the sky.
screen: `HEAVEN OR EARTH?` · `VLADIMIR COMES HOME.` · `EVERYONE TO THE RIVER.` · `ONE ROOT, TWO FAMILIES.` · then, large: `BAPTIZED IN THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Ukraine, or hold its people in mind. Sit comfortably and breathe. Let your breath move slowly, in and out, like water past a bank. With each breath out, think of one person in Ukraine you will never meet: someone waking up there today, someone far from home. If you pray, you can ask God's peace and protection for Ukraine and everyone who lives there, in whatever words you have, or with an Our Father. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, one breath at a time, the way the river keeps moving. The bell holds the time.
Kyiv's baptism. Prince Vladimir's people baptized in the Dnieper, a root shared by Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians. Today's word.
Your line: baptized in the river. Today, when you wash your hands or face, let the water remind you of a river and the people beside it. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians and Ukrainian Greek Catholics both keep a feast of Saint Vladimir and remember the baptism of Kyiv; Catholics of the Latin rite join in praying for Ukraine and for unity among Christians.

original.note: Greek: to dip, to immerse — the Gospels' word for baptizing, and a fair picture of a city in a river.

notes: Primary Chronicle: the envoys' report from Hagia Sophia ('we knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth... God dwells there among men'); Vladimir's baptism at Kherson and marriage to Anna, sister of Basil II and Constantine VIII; the summons to the river; people standing in the water to necks and chests; Vladimir's joy. All paraphrased (modern English translations are under copyright). Confirm details.
The chronicle's account of envoys visiting other religions is deliberately omitted to avoid comparing or ranking religions. The idol of Perun being thrown into the river is also omitted.
Year 988 (index title) not used in voice. 'Grand prince' title: confirm.
'Orthodox churches of Ukraine, Russia and Belarus' trace their faith to this baptism: confirm wording is fair to all, given current church divisions; Keeper may prefer a more general phrasing.
The practice prays for Ukraine without political claims; Keeper to confirm tone.
Original: Greek βαπτίζω, tied to Matthew 28:19; not a Slavonic word, to avoid an unverified spelling. Confirm.

Editor: cut the uncited 'in one morning'; the summons to the river now reports the chronicle's threat (whoever does not come, rich or poor, is the prince's enemy) instead of smoothing it over, which keeps the account fair beside day 763's forced baptisms; the practice no longer repeats the 'list of small pictures' used for days 753, 755 and 761.

Auditor (SERIOUS): 'baptism is the same word Jesus used' implied Jesus spoke the Greek word; now 'the Gospels use the same Greek word'. Hook's priests 'from Constantinople' broadened to 'the Greek lands', since the chronicle has Vladimir bring clergy from Kherson as well as those who came with Anna.
